screens.title: Index Management and Monitoring
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on the operational skills you need to manage MongoDB indexes safely and effectively. You will learn how to list and inspect indexes, remove indexes when they are no longer useful, rebuild indexes to recover space and optimize structure, and monitor index usage using MongoDB’s built-in tools. These techniques help you keep query performance high without saddling your system with unnecessary write overhead. For example, you will use the getIndexes method to verify index definitions, use the $indexStats aggregation to see how often an index is used, and use db. collection. stats to observe index sizes. A common pitfall is dropping an index without checking whether production queries depend on it; I will show how to verify usage before removal and how to recreate an index in the background to reduce impact. By the end of this lesson you will know how to make data-driven index decisions, what signals indicate an index is redundant, and how to rebuild indexes without causing unnecessary disruption. Think about a query you rely on daily and how you would confirm its supporting index is necessary — that will be your guiding question.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Index Management and Monitoring

Index Management and Monitoring

Operational skills: inspect, drop, rebuild, and monitor indexes while balancing read/write trade-offs.

In this lesson

You will use getIndexes, $indexStats, explain, and collection stats to diagnose index health and make safe change decisions.

Coming up

List indexes, measure usage with $indexStats, drop safely, rebuild with background option, and evaluate write overhead.

Explore Key Topics
Inspect
Use getIndexes and collection stats to verify index definitions and sizes.
Monitor
$indexStats and explain show usage patterns and whether an index is helping queries.
Manage
Drop or rebuild indexes carefully; use background creation to reduce write impact on large collections.
Visual Overview
Index lifecycle
Create → Monitor → Rebuild/Drop → Recreate
Monitoring signals
accesses.ops, totalIndexSize, explain output, slow query logs
Key Takeaway
Indexes improve reads but cost writes. Use data from $indexStats and explain to make safe index decisions and prefer background creation for large rebuilds.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In these two screens you will see the concrete competencies you should acquire. Each objective links a practical command with a judgement skill. First, you will learn to list and inspect indexes so you can verify names, key fields, uniqueness, TTLs, and default _id behavior. Knowing how to read getIndexes output prevents accidental misconfiguration. Second, you'll practice safely dropping indexes and learn the checks to perform before removal, including verifying usage and testing in staging. Third, you'll learn how to rebuild indexes using reIndex or drop-and-recreate patterns and when to use background creation for large collections to avoid blocking writes. Fourth, you will monitor index usage with $indexStats and db. collection. stats so you can detect unused or oversized indexes. Each objective pairs a command with a reason: you should not only run the method but interpret its output and plan an action. Finally, you will analyze the impact of indexes on write operations, learning to weigh read benefits against write cost and to remove indexes that are rarely used but expensive to maintain. These competencies help you make safe, evidence-based index decisions in production environments.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Tools

screens.title: List and inspect existing indexes
screens.narratorSegment: Listing and inspecting indexes is your first diagnostic step. The getIndexes method returns an array of index documents that describe each index's key pattern, name, uniqueness, partial filter, and additional options. For example, running db. products. getIndexes() on a products collection returns an _id_ index plus any custom indexes such as a compound index on category and price. When you inspect the key pattern, pay attention to field order and sort direction: compound index order matters for which queries are covered. The index document also indicates whether the index is unique, which will reject duplicate key values, and flags like TTL indexes which expire documents after a set time. A practical check is to compare the index key pattern against the predicates and sort clauses of your slow queries—this confirms whether a query is likely to use the index. A common misconception is to assume that an index exists because a command was run; always verify using getIndexes, because index creation can fail or be created with unexpected field order. Key takeaway: getIndexes gives you the authoritative configuration; use it before making changes and record index names so you can drop or recreate them explicitly when needed.

keyIdea.title: getIndexes is authoritative
keyIdea.text: Always verify index definitions and names with getIndexes before making changes.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › List and inspect existing indexes
Definition
What getIndexes() returns
  • Name and key pattern for each index
  • Options like unique, partialFilterExpression, TTL
  • Default _id_ index always present
Example output (simplified)
[
  { name: '_id_', key: { _id: 1 } },
  { name: 'category_1_price_-1', key: { category: 1, price: -1 } },
  { name: 'productCode_1', key: { productCode: 1 }, unique: true }
]
Inspecting details
Check key order

Field order determines which queries the index can support efficiently. For compound indexes, the left-most fields are most selective for prefix queries.

Check options

Unique and TTL flags change behavior. Unique prevents duplicates; TTL automatically expires documents.

Common mistake

Assuming an index was created without verifying its exact key pattern and name. Always confirm with getIndexes before dropping or relying on an index.

Key Takeaway

getIndexes provides the definitive configuration for each index; use it to verify names, keys, and options before any change.

screens.title: Use db.collection.stats() and indexSizes
screens.narratorSegment: db. collection. stats() is the right command when you want to quantify index storage and identify indexes that consume significant disk space. The stats output includes totalIndexSize and an indexSizes object mapping index name to its on-disk size. If you observe a very large index size with little or no usage, that is a signal to investigate. For example, some secondary indexes on high-cardinality fields can become large and contribute both to disk consumption and to write overhead for every insert or update. A practical workflow is to correlate indexSizes with access counts from $indexStats; if an index consumes substantial space but has near-zero accesses, it may be a candidate for removal. Remember that disk size alone does not imply usefulness; also check whether indexes are used in critical queries. When planning removal, snapshot the current stats, test the change in staging, and monitor query latency and explain plans. Misconception: large index size always means a bad index. Not so — an index can be large but essential for key lookup queries. The correct action is measure, cross-reference usage, and then decide.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › db.collection.stats() & indexSizes
Stats output highlights
Look for:
  • totalIndexSize — combined index footprint
  • indexSizes — per-index size mapping
  • storageSize and dataSize for context
When size is a problem

Large indexes increase disk usage and make backups and replication heavier; confirm usage with $indexStats before removing.

Example
// simplified view
db.products.stats();
// returns fields including totalIndexSize and indexSizes: { category_1_price_-1: 134217728 }
Checklist before removal
  1. Confirm low accesses.ops with $indexStats
  2. Run explain on key queries
  3. Test drop in staging and monitor latency
Key Takeaway

Index size flags candidates for investigation, but always combine size with usage metrics before deciding.

screens.title: Safely dropping indexes
screens.narratorSegment: Dropping an index can materially affect query performance, so follow a safety-first process. Start by listing indexes with getIndexes to confirm the index name and key. Next, measure usage via db. collection. aggregate([{$indexStats:{}}]) to check accesses. ops. If access is near zero and no explain plans rely on the index, proceed to test a drop in a staging environment that mirrors production workload. When you drop an index, use db. collection. dropIndex with the explicit name or exact key specification; dropping by an inaccurate name will fail, and dropping by key requires exact ordering. After the drop, re-run explain on previously indexed queries to confirm they fall back to acceptable plans or to identify necessary remedial actions. If you must recreate the index, prefer createIndex with background: true on large collections to reduce write blocking. A common misconception is that dropping an unused index is always safe; not always — some rarely used diagnostic queries may be expected during incidents. The key is to combine data from getIndexes, $indexStats, explain, and staging tests before removing anything. Your final step should be monitoring after deployment for any unexpected latency increases.

keyIdea.title: Drop with a plan
keyIdea.text: Verify name and usage, test in staging, drop explicitly, and monitor queries afterward.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Safely dropping indexes
Drop checklist
1. Confirm index

Run db.collection.getIndexes() and copy the exact index name or key pattern you plan to remove.

2. Measure usage

Use $indexStats to check accesses.ops. If the value is low for a long period, consider removal.

3. Test in staging

Drop the index in a staging copy and run representative queries. Observe explain and latency effects.

4. Monitor after drop

After removal, monitor slow queries and server logs for unexpected regressions.

Commands (examples)
// find exact name
db.products.getIndexes();
// drop by name
db.products.dropIndex('category_1_price_-1');
// or drop by key
db.products.dropIndex({ category: 1, price: -1 });
Common mistake

Dropping an index without validating its usage can cause critical queries to degrade. Verify with $indexStats and explain, and keep a rollback plan.

Key Takeaway

Only drop indexes after evidence shows they are unused or harmful. Test first, then monitor post-change.

screens.title: Rebuilding indexes and background creation
screens.narratorSegment: Rebuilding an index is useful when fragmentation accumulates or when you need to change index properties. There are two main approaches: run db. collection. reIndex() to rebuild all indexes, or drop and recreate a specific index. reIndex rebuilds every index on a collection which can be heavy; use it when multiple indexes need compaction. For single-index work, dropIndex followed by createIndex allows you to control options like background creation. Background creation reduces the impact on write availability by allowing writes to proceed during index build on replica sets and sharded clusters for modern MongoDB versions, though it still requires input and output and C P U. For very large collections, plan index builds during low traffic windows and consider offloading to a secondary where possible. A common misconception is that rebuilds are inexpensive; they are typically input and output and C P U intensive and may affect overall system performance. When recreating an index, include the { background: true } option where supported and monitor the system during the build. Finally, remember to verify the new index with getIndexes and to run explain on representative queries to ensure the recreated index meets your needs.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Rebuilding indexes
Options to rebuild
reIndex()

Rebuilds all collection indexes. Useful when multiple indexes require compaction, but is resource intensive.

Drop and recreate

Drop a single index, then createIndex with desired options. Use background creation for large datasets where supported.

Background: true

When available, background builds reduce blocking of write operations. They still consume I/O and CPU, so schedule carefully.

Command examples
// rebuild all indexes
db.products.reIndex();

// drop and recreate in background
db.products.dropIndex({ category: 1, price: -1 });
db.products.createIndex({ category: 1, price: -1 }, { background: true });
Practical tip

For very large collections, consider building the index on a secondary or during a low-traffic maintenance window and then promoting the change carefully.

Key Takeaway

Rebuilding is expensive; plan rebuilds, prefer background creation, and verify with getIndexes when complete.

screens.title: $indexStats: measuring index usage
screens.narratorSegment: The $indexStats aggregation stage reports usage statistics for each index on a collection. When you run db. collection. aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }]), MongoDB returns documents that include an accesses. ops count which shows how many times the index was used. High accesses. ops indicates a frequently used index; near-zero values across time signal a candidate for removal, especially if the index is large. Use $indexStats after running representative queries to see how accesses change. One important nuance: $indexStats measures from server start or since statistics were reset, so a low count might be due to a recent restart. Also confirm with explain() because $indexStats alone does not show whether the index is critical for a rarely-run but important operation. A practical example: run a few category-based queries, then run the aggregation to observe accesses. ops rising for your category-price index. Misconception: an index with a small accesses value is always safe to drop; instead, correlate with explain and application query traces. Combine $indexStats with db. collection. stats() to make a balanced decision about retention or removal. $indexStats: measuring index usage means use accesses.ops to quantify how often each index is used, then correlate with explain and stats.. In practical terms, use the aggregation stage to quantify index access patterns. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › $indexStats
Run and interpret
// increment usage by running queries, then:
db.products.aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }]);

// sample returned fields: { name: 'category_1_price_-1', accesses: { ops: 42 }, host: '...'}
What to look for
  • accesses.ops — frequency of index use
  • Compare ops across indexes to spot rarely-used ones
  • Correlate with restart times—stats may reset
Misconception

Low accesses.ops does not automatically mean drop the index. Confirm with explain and assess whether the index is needed for occasional but critical queries.

Quick example
Scenario

Run two category queries that should use the category-price index, then check accesses.ops to see an increase, confirming the index is actively used.

Key Takeaway

Use $indexStats to measure index access frequency and combine that data with explain and stats before changing an index.

screens.title: Using explain() to confirm index usage
screens.narratorSegment: explain() is the most direct way to verify whether a query uses a specific index. When you append explain('executionStats') to a query, the result includes a winningPlan. stage such as IXSCAN for index scans or COLLSCAN for collection scans, plus executionStats. totalKeysExamined and totalDocsExamined. For instance, running db. orders. find({ customerId: 'C123', status: 'pending' }). sort({ orderDate: 1 }). explain('executionStats') will show whether a composite index covering customerId, status, and orderDate is used. If the winning plan is COLLSCAN, the optimizer did not find a suitable index; the query will read all documents which is expensive. A concrete example: if you expect an IXSCAN but see a FETCH stage after IXSCAN, that means the index narrowed candidate keys but documents still needed to be fetched for fields not covered by the index. A common misconception is to equate IXSCAN always with good performance; an IXSCAN that examines many keys can still be slow. Always check totalDocsExamined and executionTimeMillis and compare to expected values. After examining explain output, combine the findings with $indexStats and db. collection. stats before changing index topology.

keyIdea.text: Use executionStats to see which indexes are used and how many keys and documents were examined.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › explain()
Example explain output
db.orders.find({ customerId: 'C123', status: 'pending' }).sort({ orderDate: 1 })
  .explain('executionStats');

// look for:
// winningPlan.stage: IXSCAN or COLLSCAN
// executionStats.totalKeysExamined
// executionStats.totalDocsExamined
Interpretation tips
  • IXSCAN indicates index usage; COLLSCAN means no suitable index.
  • Compare keys examined vs docs examined: large docs examined may signal inefficiency.
  • FETCH after IXSCAN means documents were still read for fields not covered by the index.
Common misconception

Assuming any IXSCAN means a query is fast. In reality, an index scan that examines millions of keys will still be slow. Check executionTimeMillis and totalDocsExamined for real cost.

Key Takeaway

Use explain to confirm whether a query uses an index and to measure the real cost in keys and documents examined.

screens.title: Server logs and slow query analysis
screens.narratorSegment: Server logs are an important passive monitoring tool. MongoDB records slow queries if their execution time exceeds the configured slowms threshold. By tuning slowms in your mongod configuration you can capture queries that would benefit from indexing. When a slow query appears in logs, use getIndexes and explain to diagnose whether a missing or inefficient index is the cause. For example, a logged query that sorts and scans many documents likely lacks a covering index ordering. Slow query logs often reveal patterns: repeated slow queries against the same collection or fields suggest candidate indexes. However, be mindful of false positives; occasional complex ad hoc queries may appear slow but not justify a global index because of write overhead. The right approach is to identify frequent slow queries, run explain, measure potential index impact, and then test the index in staging. Also consider resetting or rotating logs and correlating log timestamps with $indexStats windows to understand when usage increases. In short, use logs as a starting point, not the sole evidence for index changes. Server logs and slow query analysis means slow query logs point to index opportunities, but always corroborate with explain and usage stats before acting.. In practical terms, use slowms and logs to surface missing or inefficient indexes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. narration.text: Server logs are an important passive monitoring tool. MongoDB records slow queries if their execution time exceeds the configured slowms threshold. By tuning slowms in your mongod configuration you can capture queries that would benefit from indexing. For example, a logged query that sorts and scans many documents likely lacks a covering index ordering. Slow query logs often reveal patterns: repeated slow queries against the same collection or fields suggest candidate indexes. However, be mindful of false positives; occasional complex ad hoc queries may appear slow but not justify a global index because of write overhead. The right approach is to identify frequent slow queries, run explain, measure potential index impact, and then test the index in staging. Also consider resetting or rotating logs and correlating log timestamps with $indexStats windows to understand when usage increases. In short, use logs as a starting point, not the sole evidence for index changes. Tuning slowms

Set a threshold so the log captures queries that exceed acceptable latency for your workload.

Investigate logged queries

Run explain on queries from the log and compare with getIndexes and $indexStats to determine remedial action.

Practical workflow

  2. Run explain on the same query with executionStats.
  3. Check getIndexes and $indexStats to see if an index exists or is underused.
  4. Test index additions in staging and monitor post-deployment.
Key Takeaway

Logs reveal recurring slow queries. Use them as the starting point for explain and index analysis, not as the only evidence for index changes.

screens.title: Index impact on writes
screens.narratorSegment: Indexes accelerate reads but impose overhead on write operations. Every insert, update that modifies an indexed field, or delete requires updating all affected indexes. More indexes mean more index entries to maintain, increasing C P U, input and output, and locking pressure. This trade-off forces a deliberate decision: is a faster read worth the additional write cost? The rule of thumb is to index fields used frequently in queries that matter for latency or throughput, and avoid indexing fields that are frequently updated but rarely queried. A concrete example: an index on a message field in a high-volume logging collection that is rarely queried will enlarge totalIndexSize and contribute to write overhead for every new log entry; if $indexStats shows accesses. ops of zero, dropping that index frees space and reduces write cost. Another misconception is believing secondary indexes are free — they are not. To balance, maintain a small set of high-value indexes, remove redundant ones, and monitor the ratio of read benefits to write costs. Use staging tests and metrics such as increased executionTimeMillis or higher C P U during bursts to validate the real-world impact of index changes.

Why writes cost more
  • Insert: add entries to every index that includes the new fields
  • Update: modify index entries if indexed fields change
  • Delete: remove index entries for that document
Example

A logging collection with an index on message increases disk and write cost for every new log entry. If accesses.ops is zero, consider dropping it.

Balancing strategy

Keep indexes for queries executed often or with strict latency needs. Remove indexes used rarely but maintained on every write.

Indexes are not free. Evaluate read benefit against write overhead and keep the index set lean and focused on high-value queries.

Module 4 › Chapter 4.3 › Hands-on Activity
Step-by-step commands
use cohortia_shop;
// list indexes
db.products.getIndexes();

// run queries that should use indexes

screens.title: Common mistakes and recovery strategies
screens.narratorSegment: There are several recurring mistakes when managing indexes. First, removing an index solely because its accesses. ops is low without checking for occasional but critical queries can break important workflows. Second, dropping indexes in production without a staging trial or a rollback plan can cause prolonged outages as queries fall back to collection scans. Third, assuming background creation is free: background builds still consume resources and can slow other operations. To recover from an accidental removal, recreate the index with createIndex and, where appropriate, use background: true. If a drop caused immediate performance issues, revert by rebuilding the index and consider temporarily routing traffic or throttling writes while the index builds. For fragmentation or degraded performance, use reIndex or drop-and-recreate depending on whether you need a full compaction or a targeted rebuild. A useful habit is to keep a documented inventory of current indexes and their purpose so that recovery steps are clear. Always pair logs, explain, $indexStats, and stats to diagnose the cause rather than reacting to a single signal. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on the operational skills you need to manage MongoDB indexes safely and effectively. You will learn how to list and inspect indexes, remove indexes when they are no longer useful, rebuild indexes to recover space and optimize structure, and monitor index usage using MongoDB’s built-in tools. These techniques help you keep query performance high without saddling your system with unnecessary write overhead. For example, you will use the getIndexes method to verify index definitions, use the $indexStats aggregation to see how often an index is used, and use db. collection. stats to observe index sizes. A common pitfall is dropping an index without checking whether production queries depend on it; I will show how to verify usage before removal and how to recreate an index in the background to reduce impact. By the end of this lesson you will know how to make data-driven index decisions, what signals indicate an index is redundant, and how to rebuild indexes without causing unnecessary disruption. Think about a query you rely on daily and how you would confirm its supporting index is necessary — that will be your guiding question.

In these two screens you will see the concrete competencies you should acquire. Each objective links a practical command with a judgement skill. First, you will learn to list and inspect indexes so you can verify names, key fields, uniqueness, TTLs, and default _id behavior. Knowing how to read getIndexes output prevents accidental misconfiguration. Second, you'll practice safely dropping indexes and learn the checks to perform before removal, including verifying usage and testing in staging. Third, you'll learn how to rebuild indexes using reIndex or drop-and-recreate patterns and when to use background creation for large collections to avoid blocking writes. Fourth, you will monitor index usage with $indexStats and db. collection. stats so you can detect unused or oversized indexes. Each objective pairs a command with a reason: you should not only run the method but interpret its output and plan an action. Finally, you will analyze the impact of indexes on write operations, learning to weigh read benefits against write cost and to remove indexes that are rarely used but expensive to maintain. These competencies help you make safe, evidence-based index decisions in production environments.

This second objectives screen focuses on the practical commands and monitoring patterns you'll use day to day. You will form habits around three commands: db. collection. getIndexes to list defined indexes and inspect their key definitions; db. collection. dropIndex to remove an index by exact name or by key specification; and db. collection. reIndex to trigger a rebuild of all indexes on a collection. You will also use db. collection. createIndex with the background option to rebuild large indexes with minimal write blocking in many deployment types. Beyond commands, you'll practice monitoring with the $indexStats aggregation stage to measure accesses. ops and with db. collection. stats to review totalIndexSize and indexSizes. Finally, you'll learn to analyze explain() output to confirm whether a specific query uses an index or falls back to a collection scan. Together these skills let you identify unused or costly indexes, remove them safely, and rebuild or recreate indexes without surprise downtime. Practice these commands on a staging dataset first to see how access counts and sizes change when queries run.

Listing and inspecting indexes is your first diagnostic step. The getIndexes method returns an array of index documents that describe each index's key pattern, name, uniqueness, partial filter, and additional options. For example, running db. products. getIndexes() on a products collection returns an _id_ index plus any custom indexes such as a compound index on category and price. When you inspect the key pattern, pay attention to field order and sort direction: compound index order matters for which queries are covered. The index document also indicates whether the index is unique, which will reject duplicate key values, and flags like TTL indexes which expire documents after a set time. A practical check is to compare the index key pattern against the predicates and sort clauses of your slow queries—this confirms whether a query is likely to use the index. A common misconception is to assume that an index exists because a command was run; always verify using getIndexes, because index creation can fail or be created with unexpected field order. Key takeaway: getIndexes gives you the authoritative configuration; use it before making changes and record index names so you can drop or recreate them explicitly when needed.

db. collection. stats() is the right command when you want to quantify index storage and identify indexes that consume significant disk space. The stats output includes totalIndexSize and an indexSizes object mapping index name to its on-disk size. If you observe a very large index size with little or no usage, that is a signal to investigate. For example, some secondary indexes on high-cardinality fields can become large and contribute both to disk consumption and to write overhead for every insert or update. A practical workflow is to correlate indexSizes with access counts from $indexStats; if an index consumes substantial space but has near-zero accesses, it may be a candidate for removal. Remember that disk size alone does not imply usefulness; also check whether indexes are used in critical queries. When planning removal, snapshot the current stats, test the change in staging, and monitor query latency and explain plans. Misconception: large index size always means a bad index. Not so — an index can be large but essential for key lookup queries. The correct action is measure, cross-reference usage, and then decide.

Dropping an index can materially affect query performance, so follow a safety-first process. Start by listing indexes with getIndexes to confirm the index name and key. Next, measure usage via db. collection. aggregate([{$indexStats:{}}]) to check accesses. ops. If access is near zero and no explain plans rely on the index, proceed to test a drop in a staging environment that mirrors production workload. When you drop an index, use db. collection. dropIndex with the explicit name or exact key specification; dropping by an inaccurate name will fail, and dropping by key requires exact ordering. After the drop, re-run explain on previously indexed queries to confirm they fall back to acceptable plans or to identify necessary remedial actions. If you must recreate the index, prefer createIndex with background: true on large collections to reduce write blocking. A common misconception is that dropping an unused index is always safe; not always — some rarely used diagnostic queries may be expected during incidents. The key is to combine data from getIndexes, $indexStats, explain, and staging tests before removing anything. Your final step should be monitoring after deployment for any unexpected latency increases.

Rebuilding an index is useful when fragmentation accumulates or when you need to change index properties. There are two main approaches: run db. collection. reIndex() to rebuild all indexes, or drop and recreate a specific index. reIndex rebuilds every index on a collection which can be heavy; use it when multiple indexes need compaction. For single-index work, dropIndex followed by createIndex allows you to control options like background creation. Background creation reduces the impact on write availability by allowing writes to proceed during index build on replica sets and sharded clusters for modern MongoDB versions, though it still requires input and output and C P U. For very large collections, plan index builds during low traffic windows and consider offloading to a secondary where possible. A common misconception is that rebuilds are inexpensive; they are typically input and output and C P U intensive and may affect overall system performance. When recreating an index, include the { background: true } option where supported and monitor the system during the build. Finally, remember to verify the new index with getIndexes and to run explain on representative queries to ensure the recreated index meets your needs.

The $indexStats aggregation stage reports usage statistics for each index on a collection. When you run db. collection. aggregate([{ $indexStats: {} }]), MongoDB returns documents that include an accesses. ops count which shows how many times the index was used. High accesses. ops indicates a frequently used index; near-zero values across time signal a candidate for removal, especially if the index is large. Use $indexStats after running representative queries to see how accesses change. One important nuance: $indexStats measures from server start or since statistics were reset, so a low count might be due to a recent restart. Also confirm with explain() because $indexStats alone does not show whether the index is critical for a rarely-run but important operation. A practical example: run a few category-based queries, then run the aggregation to observe accesses. ops rising for your category-price index. Misconception: an index with a small accesses value is always safe to drop; instead, correlate with explain and application query traces. explain() is the most direct way to verify whether a query uses a specific index. When you append explain('executionStats') to a query, the result includes a winningPlan. stage such as IXSCAN for index scans or COLLSCAN for collection scans, plus executionStats. totalKeysExamined and totalDocsExamined. A concrete example: if you expect an IXSCAN but see a FETCH stage after IXSCAN, that means the index narrowed candidate keys but documents still needed to be fetched for fields not covered by the index. A common misconception is to equate IXSCAN always with good performance; an IXSCAN that examines many keys can still be slow. Always check totalDocsExamined and executionTimeMillis and compare to expected values. After examining explain output, combine the findings with $indexStats and db. collection. stats before changing index topology.

There are several recurring mistakes when managing indexes. First, removing an index solely because its accesses. ops is low without checking for occasional but critical queries can break important workflows. Second, dropping indexes in production without a staging trial or a rollback plan can cause prolonged outages as queries fall back to collection scans. Third, assuming background creation is free: background builds still consume resources and can slow other operations. To recover from an accidental removal, recreate the index with createIndex and, where appropriate, use background: true. If a drop caused immediate performance issues, revert by rebuilding the index and consider temporarily routing traffic or throttling writes while the index builds. For fragmentation or degraded performance, use reIndex or drop-and-recreate depending on whether you need a full compaction or a targeted rebuild. A useful habit is to keep a documented inventory of current indexes and their purpose so that recovery steps are clear.
